runs.t: Aviation works in UTC (also called Zulu or Z), the same time everywhere. Clients think in local time.
Every quote and trip brief shows local times and states it clearly. Check arrival dates on long flights: crossing time zones or the date line can change the arrival date.
When a client says "tomorrow morning", confirm the date, the time and the time zone in writing.

t: 0.5 Flight time, block time and positioning

runs.t: Flight time runs from take-off to landing. Block time runs from when the aircraft moves off its parking stand to when it stops at the destination. Operators may price on either; their quote says which.
A positioning leg (also called a ferry or empty leg) is a flight without passengers to bring the aircraft to the client, or back to its base. The client usually pays for it.
An empty leg is a positioning flight the operator sells cheaply. It can be cancelled or moved if the main trip changes.
A one-way trip can cost almost as much as a return if the aircraft must fly back empty.
Permits: most countries require permission for a foreign commercial flight to land or fly over them.
Slots: busy airports allocate take-off and landing times. A permit may not be issued until a slot is confirmed.
PPR (prior permission required): some airports require advance approval for parking or for the flight.
Border control: passengers pass customs, immigration and health checks. Authorities may require passenger details in advance.
Lead times vary by country and by airport, and change. The operator and its trip support know the current rules; we ask them every time.

t: 0.7 Crew duty and why trips sometimes need an extra crew

runs.t: Pilots and cabin crew may only work a limited number of hours in a duty period, set by their authority. A long flight, an early start after a late arrival, or several legs in one day can exceed those limits. The operator then adds a second crew, flies a fresh crew in, or plans a night stop. This changes the price and the schedule, so we ask early.

Fog, storms, snow, strong winds and air-traffic restrictions can delay or divert a flight. Decisions about safety belong to the captain and the operator alone. Our job is to keep the client informed and to arrange what they need on the ground.

Every person at Arche is expected to speak up about anything unsafe or illegal, and to report their own mistakes at once. Honest reports are never punished; hiding a mistake is. The director keeps a log of errors and near misses and reviews it with the team so everyone learns.

t: Module 1  Arche Executive and the broker's role

runs.t: Arche Executive is a charter brokerage registered in Singapore. We sell private flights to clients worldwide, in every region, from our base in Asia. We do not own or operate aircraft. Our value is finding the right aircraft and operator, pricing fairly, contracting safely and looking after the client from the first call to the last invoice.
Our name, Arche, is said ar-KAY. It comes from the Greek word archē, meaning origin or first principle: the point where every trip begins. Always say ar-KAY on the phone and in meetings.

t: 1.8 The Arche portal: one place for everything

runs.t: Every enquiry, quote, document, booking, payment record and commission for Arche lives in the Arche broker portal. Nothing is quoted, sold or paid outside it, and work done outside it earns no commission. The portal opens on your dashboard: your progress this month, your place in the team and every outstanding task, most urgent first.
The portal assigns organisations to brokers automatically and fairly: by country and region fit, follow-up record, conversions and fair share. Every active broker receives new leads every week.

Make first contact with every new lead within 48 hours and follow up at least every 14 days. Log every contact in the portal. A lead with no contact in time moves to the next broker with its full history. After three brokers it goes to the director.
"Not now" leads are offered again after 90 days, to a different broker with a fresh approach.
Add at least 10 new organisations a month, each with the public source where you found it. The first broker to add an organisation works it first. Duplicates are caught automatically.
Adding and updating prospects earns points on the monthly leaderboard and a bigger share of new leads. No separate fee is paid: commission rewards the booking.

Prospects are organisations and their business contacts only: no private individuals, no bought lists, no scraping, and an opt-out in every message. Anyone who opts out is "Do not contact" for everyone, for good.
These are the current settings. The director can change them in the portal; its Portal rules page always shows the ones in force.
Operations checks each trip, confirms the operator price on Avinode, completes KYC and sanctions screening, creates the Paynode payment request and issues the confirmation.

The director can give a broker booking rights, so the broker also works as operations. Nobody confirms, prices or records payment on their own booking: another operations member or the director does it.

t: Module 2  Where we may and may not sell: the legal map

runs.t: Arche sells worldwide, so we meet many sets of rules. This module gives the principles that apply everywhere, the list of flights we never sell, and a map by region. The law changes: the operator, its trip support and the official sources in Appendix D confirm what applies to each flight. When anything is unclear, the director decides before a quote is sent.
A broker arranges a flight; the operator performs it. Never describe Arche as the airline, never put our name forward as the carrier, and never let a client believe we fly or own the aircraft.

t: 2.2 What every client is told, worldwide

runs.t: We apply the strictest common standard to every client. Before the contract is signed, the client receives in writing:
That Arche Executive acts as a charter broker and not as the operator.
The operator's full legal name as shown on its AOC, and any trading name it uses.
The aircraft type, registration and year of manufacture, or "type or similar" until the tail is fixed.
The total price, what it includes, and every item that may be charged after the flight and how (Module 9).
The passenger insurance the operator carries, as confirmed by the operator, and whether Arche itself holds liability insurance.

All bookings run through Avinode, and all client and operator payments run through Paynode, so that only Arche's margin enters Arche's own account. The legal wording of our role towards the client is being settled with counsel and will be reflected in the Arche charter confirmation. Until then, use only the approved confirmation (Part A Key Booking Terms and Part B Standard Conditions), never your own wording, and never agree to change liability, cancellation or payment terms.

runs.t: Twin-engine aircraft flying far from diversion airports, for example across oceans, can need specific approval (known as ETOPS or EDTO). It can lengthen the route or require a stop. The operator plans it and confirms the routing in writing.
Pilots use a METAR (the current weather at an airport) and a TAF (the forecast). The crew and operator decide; we only watch for what may affect the client.
Fog and low cloud can delay or divert flights, often in the early morning.
Snow and ice mean de-icing, charged at cost after the flight.

t: 6.5 Operational requirements and the rules behind them

runs.t: The operator and the captain decide how each of these is handled. The rules below explain why they exist, so you ask the right questions early and tell the client what may be charged.

rows: De-icing and anti-icing
No take-off with frost, ice or snow on the wings, control surfaces, engines or sensors: EU CAT.OP.MPA.250 and US 14 CFR 135.227. Ground procedures follow ICAO Doc 9640 and SAE AS6285.
Cold, wet weather: northern winter (about November to March), southern winter (about June to September), and high or cold airports at any time
List it as an operational need, charged at cost after the flight with the receipt. Allow extra time; never promise a departure time in icing conditions.
Airport hours and night restrictions
Each airport publishes its hours and restrictions in its country's aeronautical information publication (AIP) and in NOTAMs. Many have night curfews or noise rules.
Late-night and early-morning departures or arrivals
Ask the operator whether the airport is open at that time. An out-of-hours opening may be possible at extra cost, or not at all: then change the time or the airport.
Slots and prior permission (PPR)

Busy airports are slot-coordinated (in the EU under Regulation (EEC) No 95/93, elsewhere under national rules and the worldwide airport slot guidelines). Business aviation needs a slot there too. Some airports require prior permission for the flight or for parking.
Major hubs, big events and peak seasons
The operator or its trip support requests slots and PPR as soon as the trip is booked. Never promise a time before the slot is confirmed.
Customs, immigration and private terminals

An international flight must land first at an airport with customs and immigration (Chicago Convention, Article 10). Authorities require passenger information in advance, for example eAPIS for the United States.
Every international arrival and departure
Check that customs is available at the planned time. A private terminal (FBO or VIP terminal) can cost extra. Passenger details reach the operator by its deadline.
Crew duty and rest

Limits come from the operator's authority. Example: on US unscheduled Part 135 flights a two-pilot crew may fly up to 10 hours in 24 hours, within a duty period of up to 14 hours, with at least 10 hours of rest (14 CFR 135.267). In Europe, EU flight-time rules (ORO.FTL) apply to commercial operations, and national rules still apply to some business-jet air-taxi work.
Long sectors, several legs in a day, an early start after a late arrival
Ask the operator for the crew plan in writing: extra crew, a fresh crew or a night stop. The cost is in the quote or listed as an operational need.

Crew take their rest away from the aircraft.
The aircraft waits with the client overnight or for several days
Agree with the operator whether hotel and allowances are in the price or charged at cost.
Parking and hangarage
Airports limit parking space, and some require prior permission to park. A hangar protects the aircraft from snow and ice.
Night stops and waiting days, especially at busy or winter airports
Confirm parking, or repositioning to another airport, before booking. A hangar in winter can avoid de-icing but costs extra.
Technical stops and long sectors
Range falls with load, headwinds and hot or high airports. Long flights over water can need ETOPS or EDTO approval (Module 6.3).
Very long sectors and full cabins
Only the operator confirms non-stop for that load and season. A technical stop adds time, fees and sometimes permits.
Permits

Non-scheduled flights need permission to land in, and often to fly over, other countries (Chicago Convention, Article 5, and national rules). Domestic legs on foreign aircraft are cabotage (Module 2).
Every international trip; strictest in the countries in Appendix G.5
Give the operator the full routing and passenger details at booking. Later changes need new permits and may be refused.

Entry rules for animals differ by country (in the EU, Regulation (EU) No 576/2013). Some countries accept pets only on approved routes and at approved airports.
Any animal on board
Check the destination's rules and the operator's written acceptance before quoting. See Appendix G.4.
Dangerous goods and weapons
Governed by ICAO Annex 18 and the ICAO Technical Instructions. Spare lithium batteries, oxygen, some medicines, firearms and ammunition are restricted.
Any unusual item in the luggage
Ask the client; the operator decides. Firearms and armed security need permits in every country involved: refer to the director.

Infants count as passengers on the manifest. Child seats must be acceptable to the operator. A passenger who needs medical care in flight needs an air ambulance.
Families, elderly passengers, reduced mobility
List child seats and assistance as client requests. Medical care on board is never a normal charter: refer through the director.

The caterer and the operator are responsible for food safety; they need allergies in writing.
Every flight: always ask about allergies
Write dietary needs and allergies on the order and get them confirmed back.

t: G.3 Conflict zones and airspace notices

runs.t: EASA publishes Conflict Zone Information Bulletins for European operators, and the FAA publishes prohibitions and security notices for US operators. t: H.0 How a trip moves through the portal

runs.t: Read the diagram left to right. The AI researches organisations every day and the rotation assigns them to brokers. The broker turns a lead into an enquiry, adds requests and extras and the operator quote, completes the checks and sends the trip to operations. Operations checks it on Avinode, completes KYC and the Paynode request and issues the confirmation. The client signs and pays through Paynode, the trip flies, operations records payments and the flight, and commission follows. Dashed arrows loop back: a lead with no contact in time returns to the rotation, and a trip with a problem returns to the broker.

t: 1. How is the client price calculated?

runs.t: Operator all-in price plus direct trip costs, divided by 0.91 and rounded up. Archē's margin is 9% of the price the client pays. A lower margin needs the director's approval.

25% of the charter price on signature, at least USD 2,500; the balance, including fixed-price extras, 7 calendar days before the first departure. If departure is less than 7 days away, the full price on signature. Items at cost are invoiced after the flight and paid within 10 calendar days.

t: 3. What is the difference between a fixed-price extra and an extra at cost?

runs.t: Fixed price: a supplier quoted it in writing before booking; the client pays the supplier price ÷ 0.91, rounded up, with the balance. At cost: the amount depends on the day (de-icing, extra parking, out-of-hours fees); it is invoiced after the flight with the receipt, without margin.

t: 4. Why did my lead move to another broker?

runs.t: No first contact was logged within 48 hours of assignment, or no follow-up within 14 days. The lead moves with its full history. Log every contact in the portal to keep your leads.

t: 5. How many prospects must I add?

runs.t: At least 10 organisations a month, each with the public source where you found it. Adding more earns points and a bigger share of new leads.

t: 6. Do I get a fee for prospects I add?

runs.t: No. Commission rewards the booking. Adding prospects earns points, a place on the leaderboard and a bigger share of new leads, and you work your own finds first.
Operations or the owner, after the operator price, KYC, sanctions screening and the Paynode request are done. Nobody issues, prices or records payment on their own booking.

t: 8. The airport I want is not in the list. What do I do?

runs.t: Type the four-letter ICAO code. The list holds airports suitable for jets; if it is still missing, ask operations, because the runway may be too short.

t: 9. Can a client pay by bank transfer to us directly?

runs.t: No. Clients pay only through the Paynode payment request. Never send or accept bank details by email, chat or messaging apps.

t: 10. Can I quote a domestic flight on a foreign aircraft?

runs.t: No. Domestic legs on foreign-registered aircraft are cabotage and are refused in most countries. Use a local operator for the domestic leg or redesign the trip.
It depends on the day, the aircraft and the airport. Never give a figure: list it as an operational extra at cost, and pass on the operator's written estimate only as its estimate if the client asks.

t: 12. Can a passenger bring a dog?

runs.t: Only with the destination's entry rules met and the operator's written acceptance. Some countries accept pets only on approved routes and airports. Ask before quoting.

t: 13. The client wants to change the trip after confirmation. What happens?

runs.t: Operations gets the operator's new price in writing and issues a numbered revision. Changes to routing or passengers need new permits and may be refused; any difference is paid before the flight.
For trips that have flown and whose client payment has cleared, in the month of the flight, by the 15th of the next month.

t: 15. Who sees my leads and trips?
